newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kuchma's home village unmoved by Ukraine - NATO pact.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma's home village unmoved by Ukraine - NATO pact.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma signed a security pact with NATO on Wednesday but in this sleepy village where he was born few know or care what the Western defence alliance is.

Some of Kuchma's ex-neighbours were backing him this week as he prepared to shift his former Soviet republic another step towards the West and away from Russia by acquiring a promise of negotiations with NATO if Kiev felt threatened.
But economic hardship, Kuchma's biggest headache, was the first thing on people's minds in this village on the Russian border about 350 km (200 miles) north of the capital Kiev.
"NATO? What kind of thing is this? Never heard of it," Larisa Seguta, a young mother of two said as she walked along Chaikyne's only street. "Don't remember anything like that from school."
"Know nothing about that," said Olena Moganya, 19. "Maybe you know what NATO is, Mum?"
"It's an organisation of America, England and some other countries. They are very developed. But I can't tell you any more than that," replied her mother, Nina, a teacher.
Attitudes in Chaikyne roughly reflected those of the population of 51 million, as depicted in recent opinion polls on the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
About 40 percent of Ukrainians say they do not know enough about NATO to judge or were undecided on whether joining it was a good or bad thing.

About 30 percent back Ukraine's eventual admission to NATO -- although officially the country is not yet seeking full membership and Kuchma signed a "Charter on a Distinctive Partnership between NATO and Ukraine" in Madrid.
Most of Kuchma's former neighbours work at a local collective farm named after 19th century Ukrainian poet and national hero Taras Shevchenko.
But after three centuries of domination by Moscow, they speak a mixture of Ukrainian, Russian and Belarussian.
Kuchma, born in 1938, lived here until he was a teenager, when he left for the eastern industrial city of Dnipropetrovsk.
There he attended university and made a career as the director of the local missile plant, the world's largest.
Despite campaigning on a pro-Russian platform when he was elected president in 1994, Kuchma has devoted three years in office to integrating Ukraine into Europe.
Last year he announced that Ukraine's strategy was to join the European Union.

But while establishing a strategic partnership with the West and especially Washington, which has put Ukraine third in line for cash after Israel and Egypt, Kuchma faces a tough task overcoming the economic crisis and a mountain of unpaid wages.
"I don't care about NATO or whatever. Only money bothers me," said Fedir, a builder. "I haven't been paid for months - what else am I suppose to think about?"
"NATO, MATO, TATO...What's the difference for me if I've almost forgotten what money means," said Mytrofan Kravchenko, 60, a pensioner last paid in January.

"Ukraine should make friends with everyone if it would help us to live better. But let's not allow Kuchma to turn Ukraine into a colony," he said as he cleared branches which were blown down into the road by a recent storm.
Some residents in the village, encircled by deep forest and lakes, said they backed Kiev's pro-Western stance.

"We must get closer to the rich countries. What is the sense in being friends with a beggar," Vira Gomon said as she climbed on to a bicycle. "We should move where the money and good technology are -- that is to the west, not the east".
